topicName: Aggregations, Joins, Pivoting, and Window Functions
content:
[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Advanced ETL Operations: Aggregations, Joins, Pivoting, and Window Functions"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"In modern data engineering, Extract, Transform, Load (ETL) pipelines require complex transformations to convert raw operational data into analytical insights. This tutorial covers four core pillars of data transformation: Aggregations, Joins, Pivoting, and Window Functions, utilizing PySpark as our primary engine."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Data Aggregations"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Aggregations allow us to summarize large datasets by grouping rows based on specific columns and applying mathematical functions like sum, average, count, or max."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql.functions import sum, avg, count

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("ETLTutorial").getOrCreate()

# Sample sales DataFrame
sales_df = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("2023-01-01", "North", 100),
    ("2023-01-01", "North", 150),
    ("2023-01-02", "South", 200),
    ("2023-01-02", "South", 250)
], ["date", "region", "amount"])

# Performing aggregation
aggregated_df = sales_df.groupBy("region").agg(
    sum("amount").alias("total_sales"),
    avg("amount").alias("avg_sales"),
    count("amount").alias("transaction_count")
)

aggregated_df.show()"},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Advanced Joins"},{"order":7,"type":"paragraph","text":"Joins are essential for combining datasets from different sources. In ETL, you frequently merge dimensional data with fact data using inner, outer, left, or right joins."},{"order":8,"type":"code","text":"# Sample dimension and fact DataFrames
orders_df = spark.createDataFrame([
    (1, 101, 2),
    (2, 102, 1),
    (3, 999, 5) # 999 represents a missing product
], ["order_id", "product_id", "quantity"])

products_df = spark.createDataFrame([
    (101, "Laptop", 1200.0),
    (102, "Mouse", 25.0)
], ["product_id", "product_name", "price"])

# Left Join to retain all orders even if product metadata is missing
enriched_df = orders_df.join(
    products_df,
    on="product_id",
    how="left"
)

enriched_df.show()"},{"order":9,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Pivoting Data"},{"order":10,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pivoting transforms rows into columns, which is extremely useful for generating wide reports, matrices, or feature stores for machine learning models."},{"order":11,"type":"code","text":"# Sample monthly revenue DataFrame
revenue_df = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("North", "Jan", 5000),
    ("North", "Feb", 7000),
    ("South", "Jan", 4000),
    ("South", "Feb", 6000)
], ["region", "month", "revenue"])

# Pivot month rows into columns
pivoted_df = revenue_df.groupBy("region").pivot("month", ["Jan", "Feb"]).sum("revenue")

pivoted_df.show()"},{"order":12,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Window Functions"},{"order":13,"type":"paragraph","text":"Window functions perform calculations across a set of table rows that are somehow related to the current row. Unlike regular aggregations, window functions do not collapse the rows of the DataFrame."},{"order":14,"type":"code","text":"from pyspark.sql.window import Window
from pyspark.sql.functions import rank, desc

# Sample employee salary DataFrame
emp_df = spark.createDataFrame([
    ("IT", "Alice", 90000),
    ("IT", "Bob", 85000),
    ("IT", "Charlie", 90000),
    ("HR", "David", 60000),
    ("HR", "Eve", 65000)
], ["department", "name", "salary"])

# Define window specification partitioned by department and ordered by salary descending
windowSpec = Window.partitionBy("department").orderBy(desc("salary"))

# Apply rank window function
ranked_df = emp_df.withColumn("salary_rank", rank().over(windowSpec))

ranked_df.show()"},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Best Practices for ETL Performance"},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Always filter your data (using filter or where) before performing heavy joins or window operations to minimize shuffle size."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"When executing joins on large datasets, ensure join keys are broadcasted if one of the tables is small enough to fit in memory (broadcast join)."},{"order":18,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Be cautious with pivot operations on high-cardinality columns, as they can cause severe performance bottlenecks and out-of-memory errors."}]
